title: European soccer federation votes to boycott World Cup over privatization plan
dek: UEFA's 55 European member associations voted Thursday to boycott the men's and women's World Cups unless FIFA abandons a plan to sell minority stakes in tournament commercial rights to private investors, including a firm connected to the Trump family network. FIFA has defended the proposal, saying it retains all decision-making power.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: UEFA's 55 nations collectively voted to boycott both World Cups over FIFA's plan to create a commercial company and sell minority stakes to external investors, representing the first coordinated confederation-level threat to the tournament's viability.
bottom_line: UEFA's boycott position opens the possibility of a World Cup without European participation, a scenario that would fundamentally alter the tournament's global legitimacy and commercial value. Watch whether other regional confederations (Africa, Asia, South America, Oceania) issue similar boycott threats, and whether FIFA modifies its proposal or accelerates its timeline in response to confederation pressure.
body: UEFA's 55 European member soccer associations announced Thursday that they would boycott the men's and women's World Cups unless FIFA abandons a plan to sell minority stakes in the tournament's commercial rights to private investors. The boycott threat represents an unprecedented collective action by the world's richest soccer confederation against FIFA's parent organization.

FIFA's proposal involves creating a new company to handle all commercial rights to its tournaments, including the World Cup, according to NPR reporting. The federation would then sell minority stakes in that company to private investors. Among the firms FIFA has approached is one run by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Jared Kushner, who served as senior adviser to President Trump, per NPR. The involvement of the Trump family network has placed the proposal at the intersection of sports governance and U.S. political controversy.

UEFA's formal statement articulated the federation's core objection: "Some things are simply too important to sell. The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale." The organization elaborated on the governance concern, stating that "The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in FIFA competitions, football changes forever. Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure." UEFA further warned that even minority investor presence would reshape decision-making across all competition formats, stating that every decision on the international calendar would become driven "by what best serves shareholders" rather than the sport itself.

England's Football Association immediately aligned with UEFA's position. In a statement cited by NPR, the FA said: "We stand shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues and fully support the collective view." Concacaf, the governing body for North American, Central American, and Caribbean soccer, called an emergency meeting of its 41 member associations on Thursday to discuss FIFA's proposal. Concacaf stated it was "deeply concerned by the lack of due process" and stressed that decisions affecting the game must be guided by "good governance, robust processes and long-term stewardship."

The 2030 FIFA World Cup will mark the tournament's centenary, celebrating 100 years since the inaugural edition in Uruguay in 1930. The tournament will be staged mainly in Spain, Portugal and Morocco, with centenary matches in Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay. That timeline places the boycott threat squarely in the path of FIFA's flagship event during a milestone celebration.

FIFA has defended its proposal, per NPR reporting. The organization said it would retain all decision-making power across all its tournaments and emphasized that the proposal involved only selling part of the commercial venture, not majority control. Specific governance protections or contractual commitments FIFA has offered to address concerns about investor influence are not detailed in available reporting.
